channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The IMF put hard numbers on the war-and-technology economy — global growth 3%, China upgraded to 4.6% — while Iran strikes entered a second day but markets steadied; Europe's industrial strains deepened as VW eyed plant closures and Trump moved to embargo Spain.
item.description:
• The IMF quantifies the split-screen economy: 3% global growth, inflation up to 4.7%, the war a drag and AI the offset — and China, uniquely, revised up to 4.6% (insight 2).
  • Iran conflict escalates but the market fear fades: a second day of US strikes and a blockade threat, yet Brent slipped back under USD 77 and pump-price impact is so far marginal (insight 3).
  • European industry under visible strain: VW weighs ending production at four German plants (~40,000 jobs) and Mercedes deliveries fell 8% on China — even as Berlin promises a growth plan (insights 6, 7).
  • Trade turns bilateral and coercive: Trump ordered a halt to all US trade with Spain over NATO spending, cutting across EU single-bloc rules (insight 5).
  • Defence spending hardens into industrial autonomy: NATO's Ankara deals near USD 65bn, Germany buys Tomahawks, and suppliers move to ITAR-free European production (insight 4).
Valona MIA

item.title: The July WEO Update cut 2026 world growth to 3.0% and raised inflation to 4.7%, blaming the Middle East war while crediting an AI boom — and lifted China alone to 4.6%, as the IEA, IMF, World Bank and WTO jointly warned the war's effects could be permanent.
item.description:
Yesterday's AP preview is now the full report, titled "Global Economy in the Cross Currents of War and Technology." The 3.0% figure (from 3.1% in April) sits well below the 3.5% averaged in 2024–25; 2027 is raised to 3.4%. The country detail sharpens the European picture already tracked: the euro area and Germany stay weak, Türkiye is cut to 2.9%, while the US holds up on AI. The standout is China — revised up 0.2 points to 4.6%, one of the very few upgrades, on high-tech manufacturing and export strength, echoed by World Bank data showing high-tech investment up 4.5% in January–May. Inflation is the offsetting bad news: 4.7% for 2026 (from 4.1% in 2025), easing to 3.9% in 2027, on higher energy costs and looser-for-longer worries; the UK is the bright spot, with inflation now seen back at 2% by mid-2027. Framing the release, the heads of the IEA, IMF, World Bank and WTO met on 7 July and cautioned that, while the economy has proven resilient, the war's effects on energy, food and trade are uneven and may be lasting. The forecast was largely set before this week's renewed strikes (insight 3), so risks skew down.

Industry Impact

The macro signal for ACS demand is unchanged but firmer: a two-speed world where European volumes stay soft and growth concentrates in China, India and AI-linked electronics. The China upgrade matters most — it argues against writing down Chinese industrial demand even as domestic autos slump, because the strength is in high-tech manufacturing and exports, both adhesive- and coating-intensive. Higher-for-longer inflation keeps input and energy costs elevated, pressuring margins through H2.

IMF | China Daily — inflation | China Daily — China upgrade | Cnyes | The Times of India — India/ADB | Hürriyet — Türkiye | IMF — joint statement

item.title: US forces hit Iran a second consecutive day and Trump threatened a port blockade, yet Brent fell back under USD 77 and France's pump-price impact stayed near EUR 0.03–0.04 a litre — the market is pricing a contained conflict, not a supply crisis.
item.description:
The escalation deepened: strikes hit Bandar Abbas, Sirik and Bushehr province, and Trump — speaking from the Ankara summit — called the memorandum "over," threatened renewed action and a blockade, while leaving room for talks. JD Vance framed the mission narrowly as keeping the Strait of Hormuz open. But the market reaction diverges sharply from the fear stage: after a 9% jump that briefly pushed Brent above USD 80, prices dipped for only the second time in six days, back under USD 77; shares and bonds steadied. France's petroleum union called the fuel impact "very moderate" so far, and Indian refiners said August–September crude imports are insulated by Russian, US, West African and South American barrels — though LPG remains a pressure point if Hormuz stays shut. Iran's foreign ministry says the reimposed oil sanctions violate the 18 June accord. The signal: absent a genuine, sustained Hormuz closure, this is a headline risk more than a physical-supply shock.

Industry Impact

The base case for feedstock is now firmer than the headlines suggest: expect episodic naphtha and solvent volatility around strike news, but not the sustained scarcity of a full blockade unless Hormuz closes for weeks. Keep supply-contingency plans active, but the market's own pricing supports treating spikes as tradeable noise rather than a step-change in H2 input costs. LPG-linked and Gulf-exposed chains are the ones to watch most closely.

The Guardian | Hong Kong Economic Times | MarketScreener — markets steady | Le Figaro — pump prices | The Hindu Business Line — India crude | China Economic Net — Iran MoU

item.title: NATO's summit procurement climbed toward USD 65 billion plus USD 70 billion for Ukraine; Germany agreed to buy US Tomahawks, while suppliers like Honeywell move to ITAR-free European production and Japan, the UK and Italy press ahead with the GCAP fighter.
item.description:
The USD 50 billion package tracked yesterday is now reported nearer USD 65 billion, spanning A400M transports, Saab GlobalEye early-warning aircraft, Northrop surveillance and Lockheed missiles, with USD 70 billion more pledged in equipment, aid and training for Ukraine. Two structural threads stand out beyond the headline number. First, Germany moved on national strike capability, agreeing with Washington to buy and station Tomahawk missiles — a notable deepening of German rearmament. Second, and more strategically, the supply chain is reorganising around autonomy: Honeywell Aerospace is developing products free of restricted US technology because European buyers increasingly want parts without ITAR export roadblocks, and the Japan-UK-Italy GCAP programme (targeting 2035) is explicitly designed to share cost and control outside US channels. Türkiye, whose defence and aerospace exports topped USD 11 billion in twelve months, positioned itself as a "trusted partner." Trump, still dissatisfied, kept pressing allies to spend more — the pressure that also drove the Spain embargo (insight 5).

Industry Impact

Defence is now a durable, EUR-scale European demand pillar for structural adhesives, composite bonding, sealants and specialty coatings, spanning long-cycle platforms (missiles, fighters, transports) with multi-decade sustainment. The autonomy shift is the actionable nuance: demand is tilting toward European and ITAR-free supply chains, favouring EU-based ACS suppliers and those able to qualify outside US export-control regimes. GCAP and German programmes offer particularly long visibility.

Business Standard | Lianhe Zaobao | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung — Tomahawks | MarketScreener — Honeywell | Mainichi Shimbun — GCAP | Anadolu Agency — Türkiye exports

item.title: Trump directed an immediate halt to all trade with Spain over its refusal to meet NATO's 5%-of-GDP target — his second such order — cutting across EU rules that reserve trade policy for the bloc and signalling coercive, country-by-country pressure.
item.description:
The order tasks Treasury, Commerce and the USTR with drafting a menu of Spanish products to embargo within days, so a partial ban is likely, invoked under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. It is the second time Trump has instructed Treasury Secretary Bessent to cut off Spain; after the first, in March, trade continued normally — a reason to treat the threat as leverage rather than a settled outcome. But the context has hardened: since early 2025, US actions against Spanish goods have stacked up, including steel cable, thermal paper, methionine for animal feed, aluminium sheet, steel flanges, industrial wind towers and chemical disinfection products. The move is significant less for Spain's bilateral exposure than for the precedent — Washington applying trade coercion to a single EU member to force a security outcome, testing whether Brussels responds as one bloc.

Industry Impact

The direct read-through is narrow but real: chemical disinfection products and methionine are already in the US crosshairs, and a broadened embargo would disrupt those Spanish chemical exporters and their EU customers. The larger risk is systemic — if bilateral coercion inside the single market becomes routine, supply-chain planning must price political, not just commercial, tariff risk on intra-EU-origin goods sold into the US.

Japan Today | Daily Sabah | El Correo

item.title: The Bank of France put Q2 growth at just 0.2% after a Q1 contraction, while the French risk premium over German bonds widened past 80 basis points — the highest in months — after Le Pen confirmed her 2027 presidential run.
item.description:
The recurring French-weakness story now carries a fiscal-political premium. Q2 growth of 0.2% (following ‑0.1% in Q1) rested on services — consumer services, ICT, hospitality, transport — while construction declined again, the segment most relevant to building-materials demand. The market response is the new element: the ten-year spread to German Bunds, around 60 basis points in mid-June, jumped above 80 this week as investors reprice French political risk after Marine Le Pen's announcement (the ban on her candidacy having been lifted on appeal, tracked last run). The contrast with Germany is sharpening — Berlin is adding fiscal stimulus (insight 7) while Paris faces tighter conditions and a widening deficit challenge. The eurozone's internal growth-and-risk gap is widening, not closing.

Industry Impact

Sub-1% French growth with declining construction points to soft demand for construction chemicals and industrial adhesives into 2027 in Europe's second-largest such market, with public-investment restraint hitting infrastructure-linked volumes first. Reweight European demand assumptions toward a possible German rebound rather than a broad regional recovery, and treat France as a low-growth, higher-political-risk market for the medium term.

MarketScreener — Bank of France | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung — bond spread

item.title: Merz's coalition is credited with a serious revival plan — a 2027 budget with over EUR 200 billion in new borrowing — but the VDMA warns fiscal restructuring is being deferred, and the real economy delivered VW's plan to close four plants and an 8% fall in Mercedes deliveries.
item.description:
The fiscal ambition tracked last run is now paired with a hard industrial reality check. On the plus side, Cinco Días judges the 2027 budget a genuine turn: debt-financed stimulus plus pension reform, a compulsory capitalised state pension, labour-market flexibility and deregulation. But the VDMA counters that Berlin has again postponed sustainable restructuring of EUR 555.4 billion in spending, calling it "a spending problem, not a revenue problem" that starves competitiveness investment. The ground truth is worse than the politics: Der Spiegel reports VW intends to end vehicle production at Zwickau and Emden within five years, Hannover in 2032 and Audi's Neckarsulm in 2034 — roughly 40,000 jobs — as part of 50,000 group cuts by 2030. Mercedes-Benz Q2 car deliveries fell 8%, driven by a 30% collapse in China. The stimulus is real, but so is the structural erosion of Germany's automotive core.

Industry Impact

This is the single most important demand signal for European ACS: Germany's automotive base — a major consumer of structural adhesives, sealants and coatings — is contracting structurally, not just cyclically, as production leaves and Chinese demand fades. A debt-financed stimulus could offset some of this if it flows to infrastructure and construction, so the autumn budget's composition is decisive. Plan for a shrinking German auto-adhesives pool and reallocate growth expectations toward defence, infrastructure and non-German markets.

Cinco Días — growth plan | VDMA — fiscal warning | Anadolu Agency — VW plants | Anadolu Agency — Mercedes

item.title: China's H1 passenger-vehicle exports jumped 72% to over 4.4 million units while domestic June sales fell about 26%, and the global auto aftermarket topped USD 1 trillion — the demand base is shifting decisively from new domestic sales toward exports and repair.
item.description:
The overcapacity numbers driving Europe's trade defence (insight 9) got sharper. CPCA data show H1 exports up 72% (June alone +80%), led by EVs, even as domestic June sales dropped roughly 26% to 1.5 million units; monthly production and sales still ticked up sequentially, so factories keep running and shipping abroad. Two structural shifts matter. First, the export destination fight is intensifying: a US Senate commerce committee votes on 15 July to toughen the ban on Chinese automakers with advanced connectivity and software (insight, watchlist). Second, the global aftermarket has passed USD 1 trillion, with Asia-Pacific set to be the largest regional market in 2026 and over half of China's cars now more than seven years old — a durable pivot toward repair, refinish and maintenance. The mechanism is explicit: weak home demand pushes volume outward and ages the installed base.

Industry Impact

For ACS suppliers this relocates demand along two axes: toward vehicles built in China for export markets (design-in with Chinese OEMs) and toward the fast-growing repair/refinish aftermarket (adhesives, sealants, refinish coatings) as fleets age. The offensive plays are Chinese OEM qualification and aftermarket channel exposure; the defensive variable is where Chinese export volume lands, since US and EU barriers will redirect it — potentially toward Europe — reshaping regional competition.

AP | Xinhua Daily — aftermarket | China Economic Net — production | Business Day — US ban vote

item.title: The EU's definitive 4.3%–45.3% anti-dumping tyre duties are now in force, European politicians are weighing new tools against China's "subsidised overcapacity," and Indonesia's petrochemical industry is demanding its own anti-dumping action on Chinese plastics.
item.description:
Yesterday's "measures take effect" is now enforcement with momentum. The tyre duties protect an EU sector employing 80,000 across 14 countries, and European policymakers are openly discussing additional trade-defence instruments aimed at Chinese overcapacity — while Chinese commentary pushes back, arguing competitiveness is not the same as dumping and that consumers keep buying Chinese goods. The important delta is geographic spread: Indonesia's petrochemical producers say a flood of dumped Chinese plastic feedstock is eroding margins and forcing reduced operating hours, and are pressing Jakarta for trade-security measures. The overcapacity response is no longer just a EU-China story; it is becoming a multi-front reaction across importing regions, exactly as China redirects surplus output abroad (insight 8).

Industry Impact

Tyre duties read straight through to the rubber and elastomer value chain — bonding agents, tackifiers, rubber-to-metal adhesives — where European producers gain some demand stability but face retaliation risk on EU chemical exports to China. The Indonesian plastics case is the more direct chemical-industry signal: anti-dumping action on petrochemical feedstock is spreading to ASEAN, which could firm regional pricing for local producers but raises the prospect of a fragmenting, tariff-walled global chemicals trade.

MarketScreener — tyre duties | China Economic Net — new tools | Kompas — Indonesia plastics

item.title: Canada told the USTR there is "no basis" for Section 301 forced-labour duties, and Indian industry bodies FICCI and CII urged the plan be dropped — part of over 1,500 submissions before a three-day Washington hearing that leaves the tariffs legally and diplomatically contested.
item.description:
The tariff offensive tracked last run is now a formal fight. Canada's written submission rejects any basis for Section 301 duties on its goods; India's largest industry federations argue their legal safeguards, compliance mechanisms and the damage to bilateral trade warrant withdrawal. These sit among more than 1,500 filings from industry groups and governments ahead of the hearing. The breadth of objection — allied governments and their private sectors alike — signals the measures remain litigable and unstable, a poor foundation for irreversible supply-chain decisions. The pattern connects to the Spain embargo (insight 5): the US is deploying trade coercion on multiple fronts, but the pushback is now organised and legal, not merely rhetorical.

Industry Impact

For chemical and ACS supply chains the actionable point is uncertainty, not the headline rate: with tariff levels contested and potentially unwound, the deterrent effect on investment comes from unpredictability itself. Avoid committing capital to reshoring or re-routing on the assumption these Section 301 rates will stick; treat them as a live but unsettled variable, and prioritise flexibility over one-way bets.

La Presse — Canada | The Economic Times — India

item.title: A Corporate Europe Observatory and European Environmental Bureau report finds the European Commission's Critical Chemicals Alliance — which designates molecules and sites eligible for subsidies — has been effectively taken over by the industry it was meant to scrutinise.
item.description:
Launched in January 2026 at the Chemelot park in the Netherlands, the Critical Chemicals Alliance is tasked with identifying chemical molecules and production sites deemed critical to the EU economy — a designation that can unlock EU or national subsidies. The report argues the process has been captured, steering public policy and funding toward "business-as-usual" for petrochemical and plastics producers rather than transition. Whatever one's view of the framing, the underlying signal is concrete and favourable for incumbent producers: the EU is building a mechanism to designate and subsidise strategically critical chemical capacity. This is the industrial-policy counterpart to the trade-defence tools in insight 9 — Europe is moving to protect and subsidise, not just tariff-protect, its chemical base.

Industry Impact

For chemical producers with EU operations this is a potential funding and strategic-designation opportunity worth engaging directly: sites and molecules classified as "critical" could qualify for subsidies and regulatory support. The governance controversy raises reputational and eligibility-rule risk, but the direction — European public backing for domestically critical chemical production — is a tailwind for incumbents in specialty and feedstock categories that can make the "critical" case.

EU Observer | European Environmental Bureau

item.title: Guangxi's floods killed 39 with nine missing after a reservoir breach, Super Typhoon Bavi pushed storm-impact probability to 100% across northern Taiwan, and Allianz Trade estimated a severe flood could cost the German economy up to EUR 108 billion — extreme weather is now a recurring macro-industrial risk.
item.description:
Three strands converge. In China, the Liulan Reservoir breach in Nanning's Hengzhou drove 39 deaths and 64,500 evacuations, with drones and eVTOL crews deployed for rescue — a reminder of how disaster response is itself becoming a robotics use-case (insight 13). In Taiwan, Super Typhoon Bavi lifted storm-impact probability to 100% across Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung, Taoyuan and Yilan, with warnings issued into 10 July — a direct threat to the island's electronics and semiconductor supply base. In Germany, Allianz Trade quantified the tail risk: a severe 2027 flood could cut GDP by about EUR 108 billion (~0.7%) over three years, while every euro spent on prevention avoids roughly four in damage. The through-line is that climate-driven disruption is moving from episodic to a planning assumption for industrial output and logistics.

Industry Impact

For ACS the exposures are concrete: Taiwan storm disruption threatens electronics and semiconductor customers and the specialty-adhesive and encapsulant demand tied to them; Chinese flooding hits regional construction and logistics. The German EUR 108bn estimate reframes flood resilience as a demand driver — infrastructure hardening, waterproofing membranes, sealants and protective coatings — if prevention investment follows the analysis, aligning with any construction-weighted German stimulus (insight 7).

China Daily — Guangxi | Chinatimes — Typhoon Bavi | MarketScreener — German flood cost | Global Times — rescue drones

item.title: With the World AI Conference approaching, analysts warned Europe could lose up to 40% of industrial output to a "physical AI" gap behind the US and China, as Xi pushed tech self-reliance, Chinese robot makers scaled production, and US export controls pulled top models offline.
item.description:
The AI-offset the IMF credits for cushioning growth (insight 2) has a sharp competitive edge. At Europe's first physical-AI summit, BCG's Olivier Scalabre warned up to 40% of European industrial output is at risk without a competitive industrial-AI system, as the US and China lead in embodied AI and robotics. China is moving fast on both policy and production: Xi Jinping told a national science congress the "15th Five-Year Plan" is decisive for tech self-reliance, and Shanghai's AgiBot shipped its 15,000th general-purpose robot in June — days before the World AI Conference (17–20 July) showcases the sector. The counter-current is fragmentation: Washington ordered Anthropic to block non-Americans from its most powerful models (Mythos 5, Fable 5), prompting the firm to pull them offline, and is vetting OpenAI's newest model — accelerating an open-source shift and splitting the global AI stack along geopolitical lines.

Industry Impact

Two implications for ACS. First, AI in manufacturing is where industrial demand strength concentrates — robotics, data centres and advanced electronics are adhesive-, encapsulant- and thermal-material-intensive, and China's build-out is the fastest-growing pool. Second, the European competitiveness warning is a demand risk: if EU industrial output erodes as feared, so does its ACS consumption. Position for Asian and US AI-hardware supply chains while monitoring European industrial policy as the offset.

Chinatimes — Europe warning | Xinhua Daily — Xi science congress | People's Daily — AgiBot | Asharq Al-Awsat — AI export controls

item.title: Kremlin sources say Putin is likely to escalate rather than negotiate; at the Ankara summit Trump authorised Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles; and Moscow banned diesel exports — the last unrestricted oil product — as domestic fuel shortages bite.
item.description:
Against Trump's peace push, three signals point to a longer war. Kremlin insiders describe a "high probability" of escalation, with Ukraine's drone strikes on Russian refineries and ports stiffening Putin's resolve. Trump told Zelenskyy the US will let Ukraine manufacture Patriot interceptors — a durable capability shift, not a one-off transfer, given Patriots are among the few systems able to stop Russian ballistic missiles. Most telling for the economy: Moscow imposed a full diesel export ban, the last oil product still exportable, alongside measures to ease a domestic fuel crisis — evidence that Ukrainian strikes are degrading Russian refining and squeezing supply. The war's fifth year is tightening global diesel and refined-product markets even as crude stays contained (insight 3).

Industry Impact

The direct ACS exposure is limited, but the second-order effects matter: a Russian diesel export ban tightens European and global middle-distillate supply, raising freight and logistics costs across chemical distribution, and adds another supply-security argument alongside Hormuz. Sustained conflict also locks in elevated European defence demand (insight 4) and keeps energy-cost volatility structural rather than transient — reinforcing higher-for-longer input assumptions.

The Economic Times — Putin | Lianhe Zaobao — Patriot | Forbes Russia — diesel ban

item.title: Five developing storylines with known dates: Modi's New Zealand visit, the India-UK FTA and US vote on Chinese automakers, the Iranian oil wind-down deadline, the World AI Conference, and Germany's autumn budget.
item.description:
• 10–11 July — Modi visits New Zealand: 57% of NZ exports to India go tariff-free from day one under the proposed pact; watch alongside India's just-announced removal of electronics-component import duties (Apple, Xiaomi) for India's trade momentum (insights 8, 10).
  • 15 July — India-UK FTA takes effect; US Senate committee votes on Chinese automakers: first read on specialty-chemicals market access, the same day a US committee votes to toughen the ban on software-connected Chinese vehicles (insights 8, 9).
  • 17 July — Iranian oil sanctions wind-down deadline: OFAC's revoked waiver requires buyers to end Iranian oil transactions; the real test of whether markets stay calm (insight 3).
  • 17–20 July — World AI Conference, Shanghai: China's showcase for embodied AI and industrial robotics; expect production and investment announcements feeding the physical-AI and overcapacity debates (insights 9, 13).
  • Autumn — Germany's 2027 budget to parliament: the debt-financed detail decides whether stimulus reaches construction and infrastructure — the swing factor for European ACS demand against a contracting auto base (insight 7).
Valona MIA
